decks.title: Mineral-based Industries — Part 1: Iron and steel
goals: List the raw materials of the iron and steel industry
Explain why iron and steel plants are located near coal and iron-ore fields or ports
State the location, ownership and sources of raw materials of Tata Steel, Rourkela and Visakhapatnam

slides.heading: The industry behind all industries
slides.body_md: Part 1 — rails, bridges, tractors, ships and cooking pots all need **steel**. An **integrated steel plant** handles everything from raw materials to finished steel at one site. We study what it needs, where it is built, and three famous plants.

visual.alt: Table of three steel plants with their states and ownership

slides.narration: Namaste! Rails, bridges, tractors, ships and the pots in our kitchens all need steel, so the steel industry supports almost every other industry. An integrated steel plant does everything at one site, from turning coal into coke to rolling finished steel. In this part we learn what raw materials it needs, why it is built where it is, and the story of three famous plants.

slides.heading: Raw materials of the iron and steel industry
slides.body_md: An integrated plant needs **iron ore** (mainly hematite), **coking coal** (turned into coke, which is both fuel and the agent that removes oxygen from the ore), **limestone and dolomite** (a **flux** that removes impurities as slag), **manganese** (to harden steel), **refractory materials** such as fire clay for lining furnaces, huge amounts of **water** for cooling, and **power**. Illustrative quantities per tonne of steel: iron ore 1.6 t, coking coal 0.8 t, limestone and dolomite 0.3 t, manganese ore 0.02 t — about 2.72 t of solids for one tonne of steel.

headers: Illustrative tonnes per tonne of steel

visual.alt: Table of raw materials of steel with their role and illustrative quantities

slides.narration: A steel plant needs several raw materials. Iron ore supplies the iron. Coking coal is turned into coke, which burns to melt the ore and also pulls oxygen out of it. Limestone and dolomite act as a flux, carrying away impurities as slag. Manganese hardens the steel. Fire clay lines the furnaces, and the plant also needs plenty of water and power. Altogether, nearly three tonnes of material make one tonne of steel.

slides.heading: Inside an integrated steel plant
slides.body_md: **Coke ovens** bake coking coal into coke. In the **blast furnace**, iron ore, coke and limestone are charged from the top and hot air is blown in from below; the coke burns and reduces the ore to molten **hot metal** (pig iron), and the limestone combines with impurities as **slag** (sold to cement plants). In the **steel melting shop** the carbon content is lowered and alloys added to make **steel**, which is cast and shaped in **rolling mills** into plates, sheets, rails and bars.

slides.narration: Inside the plant, coal is first baked into coke. Iron ore, coke and limestone are fed into the top of the blast furnace while hot air is blown in from below. The coke burns, the ore melts into hot metal, and the limestone carries off impurities as slag, which can go to cement factories. The hot metal is refined into steel and then rolled into plates, sheets, rails and bars.

slides.heading: Where steel plants are built
slides.body_md: Because the raw materials are **heavy and bulky** and lose much weight in processing, steel plants are built where the **cost of assembling raw materials** is lowest: **(1) near coalfields** (the Damodar valley); **(2) near iron-ore fields** (Odisha, Chhattisgarh); **(3) between the two**, so that trains carry ore one way and coal the other (Jamshedpur); or **(4) at ports**, where **imported coking coal** can be landed and steel exported (Visakhapatnam). Every plant also needs **water**, **railways**, cheap **labour** and a **market**.

nodes.label: Near coal, near ore, between them, or at a port

visual.alt: Flow explaining why steel plants are located near raw materials or ports

slides.narration: Steel plants use huge amounts of heavy raw material, and much of that weight is lost in the furnace. So they are built where raw materials can be gathered most cheaply: beside coalfields, beside iron ore mines, at a point between the two, or at a port where imported coking coal can be landed and steel shipped out. Every plant also needs water, railways, workers and buyers.

slides.heading: Worked example: weighing transport costs
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Compare the transport needed per tonne of steel at two illustrative sites, measured in tonne-kilometres (tonnes × kilometres).

**Site A (beside the ore field):** iron ore 0 + coking coal 240 + limestone and dolomite 30 + steel 800 = **1070**.

**Site B (in the market city):** iron ore 1280 + coking coal 720 + limestone and dolomite 210 + steel 0 = **2210**.

**Conclusion.** Carrying 2.72 t of raw material is costlier than carrying 1 t of steel, so site A, near the raw materials, needs about half the transport.

At site A, beside the iron ore field, we carry coal and limestone in and steel out, about one thousand and seventy tonne kilometres for each tonne of steel. At site B, in the market city, all the heavy raw materials must travel far, more than two thousand two hundred tonne kilometres. The plant near the raw materials needs about half the transport.

slides.heading: Tata Steel, Jamshedpur
slides.body_md: **Location:** Jamshedpur in Jharkhand, at the meeting of the **Subarnarekha** and **Kharkai** rivers. **Ownership:** **private sector** (Tata Steel); founded in **1907**, India’s first large integrated steel plant. **Raw materials:** **iron ore** from Noamundi (Jharkhand) and Joda (Odisha); **coking coal** from **Jharia** and West Bokaro; **manganese** from Joda; **limestone and dolomite** from Odisha and Chhattisgarh. **Other advantages:** water from the two rivers; the Kolkata–Mumbai railway; **Kolkata port** about 250 km away; cheap labour from the region.

visual.alt: Table of the location, ownership and raw materials of Tata Steel, Jamshedpur

slides.narration: Tata Steel at Jamshedpur in Jharkhand, founded in nineteen hundred and seven, was India’s first large integrated steel plant, and it is in the private sector. It gets iron ore from Noamundi and Joda, coking coal from Jharia and West Bokaro, and manganese from Joda. Water comes from the Subarnarekha and Kharkai rivers, the main railway line passes nearby, and Kolkata port is not far away.

slides.heading: Rourkela Steel Plant
slides.body_md: **Location:** Rourkela in **Sundargarh district, Odisha**, near the meeting of the Sankh and South Koel rivers that form the Brahmani. **Ownership:** **public sector** — the Steel Authority of India (SAIL); set up with **German** collaboration and commissioned in **1959**, the first integrated plant in the public sector. **Raw materials:** **iron ore** from Barsua and Kalta (Sundargarh) and Keonjhar; **coal** from Jharia and Talcher; **limestone and dolomite** from Purnapani and Birmitrapur (Sundargarh); **manganese** from Keonjhar. **Water** from the Brahmani system (Mandira dam); **power** from Hirakud.

visual.alt: Table of the location, ownership and raw materials of the Rourkela Steel Plant

slides.narration: Rourkela Steel Plant stands in Sundargarh district of Odisha, near where two rivers meet to form the Brahmani. It belongs to the Steel Authority of India and was built with German help, starting work in nineteen fifty nine. Its iron ore, limestone and dolomite come from mines in Sundargarh and Keonjhar, its coal from Jharia and Talcher, its water from the Mandira dam, and its power from Hirakud.

slides.heading: Visakhapatnam Steel Plant
slides.body_md: **Location:** Visakhapatnam on the coast of **Andhra Pradesh**. **Ownership:** **public sector** — Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Limited (RINL) **(as of the early 2020s)**; commissioned in the early 1990s as India’s **first shore-based integrated steel plant**. **Raw materials:** **iron ore** from **Bailadila** (Chhattisgarh) by rail; **coking coal** largely **imported** (for example from Australia) through Visakhapatnam port, with some from Indian coalfields; **limestone and dolomite** from Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. **Advantages of the coastal site:** a deep-water **port** for imports and **exports** of steel, and water from nearby reservoirs.

visual.alt: Table of the location, ownership and raw materials of the Visakhapatnam Steel Plant

slides.narration: The Visakhapatnam Steel Plant on the Andhra Pradesh coast was India’s first integrated steel plant built at a port. It is run by Rashtriya Ispat Nigam, a public sector company. Its iron ore comes by rail from Bailadila, but much of its coking coal is imported by sea and landed at the port next door, which also lets the plant export its steel.

slides.heading: Worked example: comparing the three plants
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Contrast the location logic of the three plants and estimate a plant’s raw-material needs.

**Jamshedpur:** between the ore of Singhbhum–Odisha and the coal of Jharia — trains can carry ore and coal both ways.

**Rourkela:** on the iron-ore, limestone and dolomite fields of Sundargarh, with coal brought from Jharia and Talcher.

**Visakhapatnam:** at a port, because it depends on imported coking coal and exports steel.

**Needs.** For an illustrative plant making 3 million t of steel a year: iron ore $= 1.6 \times 3 = 4.8$ million t; coking coal $= 0.8 \times 3 = 2.4$ million t.

visual.alt: Table contrasting the location types of the three steel plants

slides.narration: Each plant follows a different logic. Jamshedpur lies between the iron ore fields and the Jharia coalfield, so trains carry ore one way and coal the other. Rourkela sits on its own ore, limestone and dolomite. Visakhapatnam is at a port because it imports coking coal and exports steel. A plant making three million tonnes of steel needs nearly five million tonnes of ore every year.

slides.heading: From oil wells to mobile phones
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the plastic bucket, the polyester shirt, the tyre on a bus, and the mobile phone in your pocket are products of two modern industries: **petrochemicals** and **electronics**.

rows: Phones, computers, TVs, telecom and defence equipment

visual.alt: Table of the petrochemical and electronics industries with inputs and products

slides.narration: Look around. The plastic bucket, the polyester shirt, the rubber tyre and the mobile phone are all products of two modern industries. Petrochemicals are made from crude oil and natural gas. Electronics depend on components and, above all, on skilled engineers. In this part we look at what these industries make, where they are, and why they matter so much today.

slides.heading: What petrochemicals are
slides.body_md: **Petrochemicals** are chemicals made from **crude oil** and **natural gas**. At a **refinery and cracker**, oil fractions such as naphtha, or natural gas, are broken down into basic building blocks such as **ethylene, propylene and benzene**. These are joined into long chains (**polymers**) and other compounds to make **plastics** (polyethylene, PVC), **synthetic fibres** (polyester, nylon, acrylic), **synthetic rubber**, **detergents**, **paints**, **solvents**, dyes, and raw materials for **fertilisers** and **medicines**.

visual.alt: Flow from crude oil and natural gas to building blocks to petrochemical products

slides.narration: Petrochemicals are chemicals made from crude oil and natural gas. In a refinery and cracker, oil or gas is broken into simple building blocks such as ethylene and propylene. These are linked into long chains called polymers to make plastics, synthetic fibres like polyester and nylon, and synthetic rubber. Other petrochemicals become detergents, paints, solvents and raw materials for medicines and fertilisers.

slides.heading: Why petrochemicals matter
slides.body_md: **Relevance:** petrochemical products are **cheap, light, strong, durable and resistant** to water and rust, so they **replace wood, metal, glass, cotton and jute** in many uses. **Agriculture:** irrigation pipes, drip lines, mulch sheets, fertilisers and pesticides. **Health:** syringes, blood bags, medicine packaging. **Daily life:** clothes, footwear, furniture, packaging, paints, detergents. **Industry:** tyres, cables, vehicle parts. The industry gives **employment** and **export** income. **Concerns:** most plastics are **not biodegradable**, so careless disposal pollutes land, rivers and seas — recycling and responsible use are essential.

slides.narration: Why do petrochemicals matter? Their products are cheap, light, strong and long lasting, so they replace wood, metal, glass and natural fibres. Farmers use plastic pipes and drip lines, hospitals use syringes and blood bags, and we wear polyester and walk on synthetic soles. But most plastics do not rot, so careless disposal pollutes land, rivers and seas. Recycling and careful use are essential.

slides.heading: Worked example: why Gujarat’s coast attracts petrochemicals
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Explain why the coast of Gujarat, from Jamnagar to Hazira and Dahej, has become India’s leading petrochemical region.

**Step 1. Raw material.** Large refineries at Jamnagar and Koyali, and natural gas from offshore fields and import terminals, supply feedstock on the spot.

**Step 2. Ports.** Deep-water ports handle imported crude oil and export finished products.

**Step 3. Linked industries.** Textile mills of Surat and Ahmedabad buy synthetic fibres; plastics and chemical units cluster nearby.

**Step 4. Policy and capital.** Industrial estates, special economic zones and private investment.

visual.alt: Flow of four factors leading to the Gujarat coast petrochemical belt

slides.narration: Why is the Gujarat coast India’s petrochemical hub? Big refineries at Jamnagar and Koyali, and natural gas brought by sea and pipeline, supply the raw material right there. Deep water ports bring in crude oil and ship out products. The textile mills of Surat and Ahmedabad buy synthetic fibres, and industrial estates and private investment have helped many plants grow side by side.

slides.heading: Worked example: reading output shares
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The imagined complex makes 1200 thousand tonnes a year. (a) What share is plastics? (b) If synthetic-fibre output rises by 60 thousand tonnes while the rest stays the same, what will its new share be?

**(a)** $\frac{600}{1200} \times 100 = 50$%.

**(b)** New fibre output $= 240 + 60 = 300$; new total $= 1200 + 60 = 1260$; share $= \frac{300}{1260} \times 100 = 23.8$%.

slides.narration: Plastics make six hundred of the twelve hundred thousand tonnes, so their share is fifty per cent. If fibre output grows by sixty thousand tonnes, it becomes three hundred, and the total becomes twelve hundred and sixty. Dividing three hundred by twelve hundred and sixty and multiplying by one hundred gives a new share of about twenty three point eight per cent.

slides.heading: The electronics industry and its relevance
slides.body_md: **Products:** mobile phones, computers, televisions, telecom equipment, medical equipment, satellites and **defence electronics**, and components such as circuit boards. **Relevance in the modern world:** it underpins **communication**, banking, education, health care, transport and governance (digital services); it is vital for **defence and space**; it is closely linked to the **information technology (IT)** and software industry; it gives jobs to many skilled young people and earns **exports**. It needs little raw material but much **skill, research and capital**, so it is a **footloose** industry that can locate near educated workers and good infrastructure.

sections.heading: 1. Integrated iron and steel plants: raw materials
sections.body_md:
- **Integrated plant:** all stages at one site — coke ovens, blast furnace, steel melting shop, rolling mills.
- **Raw materials:** iron ore (mainly hematite); coking coal (coke: fuel and reducing agent); limestone and dolomite (flux, removes impurities as slag); manganese (hardens steel); refractories (fire clay, quartzite); water; power.
- **Illustrative needs per tonne of steel:** iron ore 1.6 t, coking coal 0.8 t, limestone and dolomite 0.3 t, manganese ore 0.02 t — about 2.7 t of solids.
- **By-product:** slag, used to make cement.

key_terms.definition_md: A plant that carries out every stage of steel making, from raw materials to rolled steel, at one site.
A substance such as limestone that combines with impurities in the furnace to form slag.
A hard fuel made by heating coking coal without air; it melts and reduces iron ore.

visual.alt: Table of steel inputs and their roles

sections.heading: 2. Location of iron and steel plants
sections.body_md:
- Raw materials are heavy and bulky and lose weight in smelting, so plants are built where raw materials can be assembled most cheaply.
- **Near coalfields** (Damodar valley), **near iron-ore fields** (Odisha, Chhattisgarh), **between the two** (two-way rail traffic, Jamshedpur), or **at ports** (imported coking coal, exports — Visakhapatnam).
- Also needed: water, railways, labour, market, capital.
- **Tonne-kilometres** = tonnes carried × distance; the lower the total, the cheaper the site.

key_terms.definition_md: A unit of transport work: one tonne carried one kilometre.

- **Relevance:** cheap, light, durable substitutes for wood, metal, glass and natural fibres; uses in farming, health, clothing, transport; jobs and exports.
- **Concern:** plastics are not biodegradable — recycle and reduce.

**Common mistakes**
- Calling limestone a fuel (it is a flux).

questions.stem_md: Explain, with an Indian example of each, why an integrated steel plant may be located (a) between coal and iron-ore fields, (b) on an iron-ore field, and (c) at a port.

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.solution_md: Raw materials; roles; location; 6.4, 3.2, 1.2 million t.

(d) It was India’s first integrated steel plant built on the coast, beside Visakhapatnam port. The port lets it import coking coal by sea and export steel, while iron ore comes by rail from Bailadila; nearby reservoirs supply water.

questions.stem_md:
Per tonne of steel, illustrative tonnages carried are iron ore 1.6 t, coking coal 0.8 t, limestone and dolomite 0.3 t and finished steel 1 t. Site A lies beside an iron-ore field (iron ore 0 km, coking coal 300 km, limestone and dolomite 100 km, steel 800 km). Site B lies in a large market city (iron ore 800 km, coking coal 900 km, limestone and dolomite 700 km, steel 0 km).

(a) Calculate the total tonne-kilometres per tonne of steel at site A. [2]

(b) Calculate the same for site B. [2]

(c) Which site should be chosen? Explain your answer using the idea of weight loss. [3]

(d) Visakhapatnam was built at a port rather than beside an ore field. Using this method, explain what change in the inputs makes a port site the cheaper choice. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A $= 0 + 240 + 30 + 800 = 1070$ tonne-km.

(b) B $= 1280 + 720 + 210 + 0 = 2210$ tonne-km.

(c) Site A, which needs about half the transport. About 2.72 t of inputs are needed for each tonne of steel, and most of that weight is lost in the furnace, so it is cheaper to carry the single tonne of steel to the market than the heavy inputs to the city.

(d) When coking coal is imported, it arrives by sea; at a port it needs no inland haul, while at an inland ore field it would have to be carried hundreds of kilometres by rail. Iron ore can come by rail (Bailadila) and steel can be exported from the same port, so the total tonne-kilometres become lowest at the port.

questions.solution_md: A 1070; B 2210; choose A; imported coal favours a port.
